introduction: These readings hold that material civilization is a lamp-glass and divine civilization the lamp: invention, wealth and learning are means, and without a moral and spiritual life they serve war and misery as readily as well-being. A hundred of the guide's quotations are read here beside a hundred from other scriptures, poets and thinkers. Most stand alongside: prophets and psalmists on plenty without satisfaction, the Gospels on gaining the whole world, Goldsmith, Wordsworth, Thoreau, Arnold and Mill on an age rich in means and poor in ends. Some push back or add a side: Darwin, Lucretius, Heraclitus and Marx speak for an account of the world without spirit, and Whitman, Hopkins and Paul ask whether material achievement and the goodness of people without religion belong inside the picture.
questions: The readings call material civilization the glass and divine civilization the lamp. What would each look like in a city you know, and which is easier to see?
Haggai, Thoreau and Mill all describe plenty and invention that do not satisfy. What do the readings say is missing, and do the three agree?
Darwin finds between human beings and animals a difference of degree and not of kind; the readings find a difference of kind. What follows in daily conduct from each view?
Paul speaks of people who without the law do by nature what it contains. How do the readings account for the goodness of people who hold no religion?
Marx called religion the opium of the people. What kind of religion would deserve that charge, and what kind do these readings ask for?
Where in your own work or study are improved means serving an unimproved end, and what would change that?

outside.why: Jesus asks what it shall profit a man to gain the whole world and lose his own soul.
Deuteronomy says that man does not live by bread only, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of the Lord.
The Qur'an's similitude has the same parts: a niche wherein is a lamp, and the lamp in a glass.
Goldsmith says that ill fares the land where wealth accumulates and men decay.
In the parable a rich man fares sumptuously every day while a beggar full of sores lies at his gate.
The Preacher looked on all the works his hands had wrought and found vanity and vexation of spirit.
Arnold called faith in machinery, as if it had a value in and for itself, his age's besetting danger.
Revelation addresses a church that says 'I am rich, and increased with goods' and does not know that it is poor and blind.
The psalm says that except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain.
Tennyson says of his own age that knowledge comes, but wisdom lingers.
Mill held that the worth of a State, in the long run, is the worth of the individuals composing it.
UNESCO's constitution says that since wars begin in the minds of men, the defences of peace must be constructed there.
Emerson says in his ode that things are in the saddle, and ride mankind.
Thoreau calls our inventions pretty toys: improved means to an unimproved end.
Haggai describes plenty without satisfaction: ye eat, but ye have not enough, and earn wages to put into a bag with holes.
Eisenhower said that every gun made and every warship launched is a theft from those who hunger and are not fed.
Isaiah foresees the metal of war beaten into plowshares and into pruninghooks, and war learned no more.
Mary Shelley's Frankenstein warns by his own example how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge. What separates the graduate who serves from the graduate who harms?
Huxley held that the ethical progress of society depends on combating the cosmic process, not imitating it.
Jeremiah blames those who say peace, peace, when there is no peace.
Jesus says that a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
The psalm says: put not your trust in princes, whose thoughts perish in the day their breath goes forth.
Twain's stranger spells out what a congregation has also asked for in praying for victory. What would newspapers of slaughter look like if read with his eyes?
Arnold sees a world that has really neither joy, nor love, nor light, where ignorant armies clash by night.
Twain, writing in 1901, called the powers of Christendom members of a Blessings-of-Civilization Trust.
Thoreau says that the mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.
Thoreau went to the woods to live deliberately and front only the essential facts of life.
Wordsworth says in his sonnet that getting and spending, we lay waste our powers.
Jesus says to a busy host: thou art careful and troubled about many things, but one thing is needful.
Jesus says that no man can serve two masters: ye cannot serve God and mammon.
The prayer in Proverbs asks to be given neither poverty nor riches, only food that is convenient.
Shakespeare's king says that within the hollow crown Death keeps his court.
Shelley's traveller finds a king's boast on a pedestal, and round the decay the lone and level sands.
The rich man in the parable is told: this night thy soul shall be required of thee.
Isaiah describes a land full of silver and gold that worships the work of its own hands.
Jesus says: where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Whitman read God's purpose in the engineering of his America: the earth spanned, the lands welded together. Is material achievement a rival to spiritual life, or an unfinished part of it?
Montesquieu's Persian visitor reports that in Paris no one walks: they run, they fly.
John's letter says that the world passeth away, and the lust thereof.
Yeats wrote of Europe that things fall apart and the centre cannot hold.
The Qur'an says of the heedless that they know only some appearance of the life of the world.
The Qur'an says that rivalry in worldly increase distracts people until they come to the graves.
Kipling says that East and West shall never meet, and then that they do when two strong men stand face to face. What have both hemispheres forgotten, according to the guide, that would let them meet?
Burke said that his countrymen cherish their old prejudices instead of casting them away.
Heraclitus says that no one of gods or men made this ordered world: it was ever an ever-living Fire. How should a believer in design answer the oldest form of the materialist's claim?
Paul says that the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made.
Darwin writes of man with all his noble qualities, sympathy and benevolence. Is an account of human origins in nature a denial of those qualities, or a way of wondering at them?
The psalm says: be ye not as the horse, or as the mule, which have no understanding.
The Preacher says that as the beast dies so dies the man, and all go unto one place.
Whitman thinks he could turn and live with animals, so placid and self-contained, who do not whine about their condition. What do the animals have that he envies, and is it materialism?
Darwin held that the difference in mind between man and the higher animals is one of degree and not of kind. What is at stake, for the guide, in that sentence?
Paul says that the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit, for they are spiritually discerned.
Hamlet says that there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in philosophy.
Paul says that those who have not the law and do by nature what it contains are a law unto themselves. What does the guide make of people who do good without religion?
In the parable the one who showed mercy was a Samaritan, outside the fold of those who passed by. What does it mean that lovers of peace are so often found among freethinkers?
Proverbs says that better is little with the fear of the Lord than great treasure and trouble therewith.
Paul quotes a call to the sleeper: awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead.
Revelation tells a church that it has a name that it lives, and is dead.
Marx called religion the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, the opium of the people. What in the religion of his day gave his sentence its force?
Tennyson's bells ring out the old and ring in the new, ring out the false and ring in the true.
Prospero calls the cloud-capped towers and gorgeous palaces a baseless fabric that shall dissolve.
Paul speaks of those who worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator.
The psalm says of idols, the work of men's hands, that they have eyes and see not.
Jesus warns against casting pearls where they will only be trampled under foot.
Paul says that the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.
Jesus says that in the days of Noah they ate, drank and married until the flood came.
Jesus says that what is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Arnold hears the sea of faith, once at the full, in a melancholy, long, withdrawing roar.
Hosea says in the name of God that a people is destroyed for lack of knowledge.
Moses sets two ways before the people, life and death, and tells them to choose life.
Gandhi judged modern civilization to be such that one has only to be patient and it will be self-destroyed.
Kipling wrote that all our pomp of yesterday is one with Nineveh and Tyre.
Proverbs sends the sluggard to the ant, to consider her ways and be wise. Is the busyness of a great city like that of bees and ants a reproach, or a virtue lacking only a purpose?
Marcus Aurelius says that what is not good for the swarm is not good for the bee.
Pascal says in the Pensées that man is neither angel nor brute, and warns the would-be angel.
Aristotle says that man, when perfected, is the best of animals, and when separated from law and justice, the worst.
Tennyson bids us move upward, working out the beast, and let the ape and tiger die.
Plato pictures human beings living in an underground den, chained so that they see only what is before them.
Dickens opens with an age that was at once the age of wisdom and the age of foolishness.
Wordsworth says that the world is too much with us, late and soon.
Jesus foresees that because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold.
The psalm says that the fool hath said in his heart, there is no God.
Hosea's God says of his people: they knew not that I healed them.
Isaiah complains of his own people that the ox knows his owner, but they do not consider.
John says that the light shineth in darkness, and the darkness comprehended it not.
Jeremiah says that the heart is deceitful above all things, and asks who can know it.
Hopkins says that the world is charged with the grandeur of God and asks why men do not reck his rod. If the grandeur is there, what keeps a prosperous people from seeing it?
Amos says to the comfortable of his day: woe to them that are at ease in Zion.
Isaiah says that the whole head is sick, and the whole heart faint.
Jesus says that unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.
Lucretius said two thousand years ago that the time after death will be nothing to us, as the time before birth was. Is the materialism of modern Europe new, and does its age count for or against it?
The Preacher says that there is no new thing under the sun.
Ezekiel is told to call the breath from the four winds upon the slain, that they may live.
Job says that these are only parts of his ways, and how little a portion is heard of him.
Zechariah hears: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Paul says that they that are after the flesh do mind the things of the flesh.
The Lord's Prayer asks that the will be done in earth as it is in heaven.
Mill doubted whether all the mechanical inventions yet made had lightened the day's toil of any human being.
Keats says that philosophy will clip an angel's wings and put the rainbow in the dull catalogue of common things.
Whitman leaves the astronomer's charts and diagrams to look up in perfect silence at the stars.

romans-a-law-unto-themselves.text: For when the Gentiles, which have not the law, do by nature the things contained in the law, these, having not the law, are a law unto themselves: Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness, and their thoughts the mean while accusing or else excusing one another

romans-worshipped-the-creature.text: Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen
